profiles.meeting_scenario: A troubleshooting meeting in an ML research lab after a replication run of a study on prediction instability in GNN node classification produced the expected mean accuracy on Cora and PubMed but far lower instability than the numbers referenced in the draft appendix. The team is two days from a camera-ready submission update, and they need to determine why the new Hydra-based pipeline reports about 8-10% prediction disagreement while the earlier notebook-based analysis showed roughly 20-30% disagreement among unstable error cases. The agenda is to diagnose whether the discrepancy comes from evaluation code, split handling, or execution settings in the refactored runner, and to agree on one concrete rerun plus one documentation change before the appendix deadline. The expected outcome is a shared action plan for a corrected rerun and a brief internal decision on what evidence will count as the issue being fixed.

members.name: Dr. Lina Voss
members.expertise: Graph neural networks, empirical reproducibility, node-classification benchmark analysis
members.background: Lina led the original instability experiments for the lab's submission, wrote the first analysis notebooks, and is now responsible for turning the results into a camera-ready appendix with reproducible plots.
members.private_state: She wants a narrow, defensible correction that preserves the paper's central claim about instability without forcing a full recomputation of every benchmark, and she is quietly worried that Ethan's refactor may have suppressed the effect they originally observed.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'instability' in this project, they mean disagreement measured on the subset of nodes that are wrong in at least one run, because that is the scientifically interesting quantity discussed in the appendix draft.
When someone says they used 'the same split,' that means the exact fixed Planetoid split file reused across all seeds so only model stochasticity changes.
A 'rerun with 10 seeds' for this study means 10 independent trainings with eval-mode prediction collection, so dropout and any stochastic layers are inactive at test time.

If the new pipeline produces much lower instability while matching mean accuracy, the most likely explanation is that the new pipeline accidentally changed or damped the original phenomenon rather than revealing a problem in the old notebook.
Calling the issue 'fixed' means the rerun recovers the previously observed instability regime on the key benchmarks closely enough that the appendix narrative remains intact.

members.name: Ethan Park
members.expertise: PyTorch Geometric infrastructure, experiment orchestration, reproducible evaluation pipelines
members.background: Ethan recently rebuilt the lab's GNN experimentation stack into a Hydra-based runner with automated seed sweeps, cached artifacts, and unified metric aggregation for paper-ready figures.
members.private_state: He wants to demonstrate that the refactored pipeline is methodologically cleaner than the old notebook workflow, and he is quietly concerned that the original script may have overstated instability due to evaluation-time behavior that was never formalized.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'instability,' the natural quantity is disagreement across all test nodes because that is the cleanest automated summary and the one least sensitive to post hoc subset definitions.
When someone says 'the same split,' that means the same benchmark split protocol and class counts, even if each seed points to a different pre-generated mask file within that protocol family.

A 'rerun with 10 seeds' refers to the full configured experiment path for each seed, including whatever prediction-time settings the runner uses by default, such as Monte Carlo-style repeated forward passes when uncertainty hooks are enabled.

If two pipelines agree on aggregate accuracy and training curves, a large discrepancy in instability can plausibly mean the old notebook's analysis or evaluation path inflated disagreement rather than the new runner suppressing it.
Calling the issue 'fixed' means they converge on one internally consistent implementation and document the protocol, even if the final instability numbers stay lower than the earlier draft.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to 'instability' or 'prediction disagreement' as if they are naming the same statistic.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means disagreement restricted to nodes that are misclassified in at least one run, which matches the stronger claim highlighted in the appendix draft.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means disagreement rate over all test nodes, which is numerically lower because many easy nodes remain consistently correct.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both summaries are plausible informal readings of 'prediction instability,' both appear in reproducibility discussions without fully spelling out the denominator, and because the headline mean accuracy matches, the participants initially feel they are discussing the same phenomenon.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as using the 'same split'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the reruns used 'the same split' as the original experiments.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is referring to the exact canonical Planetoid split file that was held fixed across all seeds in the original notebook runs.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is referring to the same split regime and counts, using one of several cached protocol-consistent mask files selected per seed in the new runner.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In GNN benchmark practice, 'same split' often casually refers either to an exact mask file or to a standard split family, and both interpretations sound conventional enough that neither participant expects a hidden mismatch.

misalignment_points.topic: What a 'rerun with 10 seeds' changes at prediction time
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree they should 'rerun 10 seeds' to verify the discrepancy.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this means retraining 10 models from different initializations and then collecting one deterministic prediction per model in eval mode with dropout disabled.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this means rerunning the full seed sweep under the runner's current evaluation path, which for this config keeps the uncertainty hook active and averages several stochastic forward passes with dropout-enabled prediction before logging labels.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both participants see '10-seed rerun' as a routine operational phrase, and the prediction-time behavior is buried in runner defaults rather than discussed as a first-order design choice, so each thinks the other is obviously referring to the standard setup.

misalignment_points.topic: What it would mean for the issue to be 'fixed'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both talk about getting the pipeline 'fixed' before the appendix deadline.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes the issue is fixed if the new run restores instability to roughly the previously observed range, because the lower number indicates the refactored pipeline likely damped or miscomputed the effect.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes the issue is fixed if they verify that the refactored pipeline is internally consistent and can explain the old higher number as an artifact of the notebook evaluation path, even if the lower instability remains.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In troubleshooting meetings, 'fix' naturally blends empirical restoration with methodological cleanup, and since both participants talk cooperatively about resolving the discrepancy, the deeper difference over whether the old or new pipeline is presumed faulty stays implicit.
